seoDesc: Law of cosines: work out side c (Triangle solution) from the side a and the side b. A free math calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Law of cosines calculator turns the side a and the side b into side c (Triangle solution). It suits a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Law of cosines calculator work?
sections.html:
The Law of cosines calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports side c (Triangle solution) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the given); then you type in the side a (Known values), the side a (Known values), the side b (Known values) and the side b (Known values).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

sections.title: The formula behind the Law of cosines calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Side c=(the square root of ((side a ^ 2) − 2 × side a × side b × the cosine of (angle γ) + (side b ^ 2)))
Angle α=(((1 ÷ 2) × (-(side a ^ 2) + (side b ^ 2) + (side c ^ 2)) ÷ (side b × side c)))
Angle β=(((1 ÷ 2) × ((side a ^ 2) − (side b ^ 2) + (side c ^ 2)) ÷ (side a × side c)))
Angle γ=(((1 ÷ 2) × ((side a ^ 2) + (side b ^ 2) − (side c ^ 2)) ÷ (side a × side b)))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Given set to SAS (2 sides + angle between), Side a = 30 cm, Side b = 30 cm and Angle γ = 10 deg. The calculator returns Side c = 5.229345 cm, Angle α = 60 deg, Angle β = 60 deg and Angle γ = 60 deg.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Side c = 5.229345 cm, Angle α = 60 deg, Angle β = 60 deg and Angle γ = 60 deg should be roughly the size you expected from Given set to SAS (2 sides + angle between) and Side a = 30 cm.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Law of cosines calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a homework answer before you hand it in
  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the side a and the side b — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Law of cosines calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns side c (Triangle solution), derived from the side a and the side b. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Law of cosines calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the side a and the side b, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter side a (Known values) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Side a (Known values) opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Side c = 5.229345 cm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Law of cosines calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
